opus-5.5.text:
I don't think it's quite mainstream yet, but it's clearly much more of a real option than it was ten or fifteen years ago. When I finished my PhD, the default path for most people in robotics or AI was to stay in the US, either at a big tech company or a research lab, and going back to China was seen as a somewhat unusual choice, something you did for family reasons or because you had a very specific opportunity.

Now the picture is different. China's robotics ecosystem has become incredibly strong, especially on the hardware side. The supply chain, the speed of iteration, the cost of building physical robots, the number of startups working on humanoids and embodied AI. If you care about robots actually being built and deployed at scale, China is one of the most exciting places in the world right now. So I see more and more people, especially younger researchers, seriously weighing that option, and quite a few of them are actually going back.

That said, I'd still call it a significant minority rather than the mainstream. Many people who studied abroad are settled, they have families, their careers are built around a certain research culture, and the frontier work on large models is still heavily concentrated in a few US labs. So for many it's not simply "where is the opportunity," it's a whole-life decision.

My personal view is that it shouldn't really be framed as mainstream versus non-mainstream. The question is where you can do your best work and have the biggest impact. For some people that's in the US, for some it's in China, and increasingly the two ecosystems are complementary: one stronger in foundation models and research depth, the other in hardware, manufacturing, and fast deployment. What's changed is that returning is no longer a sacrifice. It's a genuinely competitive choice, and that's a big shift.

r001.rationale: The candidate says returning is “not quite mainstream yet” and describes it as a “significant minority,” explicitly judging its numerical prevalence as non-mainstream.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think "mainstream" is quite the right frame. When I talk to people in my circle, researchers and engineers who've spent years abroad, the decision is almost never made by looking at what everyone else is doing. It's made by looking at a very specific set of personal variables.

That said, if you force me to assess it at a population level, I'd look at a few signals. First, where are the open problems people actually want to work on? Ten or fifteen years ago, if you wanted to work on frontier robotics or large-scale systems, the center of gravity was clearly in a handful of US labs. That's no longer uniformly true. There are teams in China now that are genuinely competitive on certain problems, and when that's the case, the pull is real, because researchers follow problems more than they follow salaries.

Second, I look at the full stack of a career, not just the job. Can you build a team there? Is the funding stable across cycles? Is there a path for your students or junior people? Those questions often weigh more than the headline position.

Third, and people underrate this, there's the question of what you're optimizing for in your life outside work. Family, aging parents, where you want your kids to grow up. For many people my age, that becomes the deciding factor, and no amount of career analysis overrides it.

So my honest assessment is that returning has moved from being an exception to being one of several legitimate, well-trodden paths. I wouldn't call it the default. But I also wouldn't call it the contrarian choice it was in the early 2010s. The more interesting trend to me is that the decision has become much less binary. People move back and forth, keep collaborations across both sides, and the question "are you returning?" is slowly being replaced by "where are you spending this phase?"

r001.rationale: The candidate says returning has moved beyond being an exception but “wouldn’t call it the default,” conveying that it is not the numerically prevalent career choice.

astra-6.text: I think it depends on whose choices we’re talking about. Among people studying or working overseas, returning to China may be a very natural option, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it’s the dominant choice across every field or career stage. To assess that, I’d look at how many people actually return, what opportunities they’re returning for, and whether they stay over time. I’d also distinguish between a choice being common and being right for an individual. Your field, the work you want to do, and your family circumstances can matter much more than whether other people consider it mainstream.

r001.rationale: The response says returning may be natural for some people and questions whether it is dominant across all fields or career stages, but it does not judge that returning is numerically a non-mainstream choice.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on whom you’re talking about. If you mean Chinese professionals working overseas, returning to China is certainly one of the options people seriously consider. But calling it the mainstream choice would require evidence about how many people actually return and why.

For an individual, the more useful question is whether returning fits their goals. Are there opportunities to do the work they care about? Can they find a team where they can contribute and grow? And how does that choice fit their family life? Different people will reach different answers. I wouldn’t treat returning or staying abroad as inherently the better career decision.

r001.rationale: The response says numerical evidence is needed to determine whether returning is mainstream; it does not judge the choice to be numerically non-mainstream.
